explanations.D: Wrong part: both premises and the conclusion are universal; nothing corresponds to the stimulus's 'some.'
explanations.E: Wrong force: two 'most' premises replace 'all' and 'some'; the conclusion happens to follow, but the quantifiers do not match.

keyTakeaway: Check which term the two premises share: in 'all A are B; some A are C,' both are about A, and the conclusion links B and C.
predictionHint: All A are B; some A are C; so some B are C.

stimulus: Vaccinating most of a herd against a contagious disease protects even the unvaccinated animals, because the disease cannot spread readily through a population in which most individuals are immune. Computer viruses, like contagious diseases, spread only from one susceptible machine to another. So installing protective software on most of a network's machines should protect even the unprotected ones.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Vaccinating most of a herd protects even the unvaccinated animals. So vaccinating most of a human population will protect even the unvaccinated people.
choices.B: Rotating crops prevents the buildup of pests in a field, because pests that specialize in one crop cannot survive a season of a different crop. Parasites of grazing animals, like crop pests, specialize in a single host species. So alternating cattle with sheep on a pasture should prevent the buildup of parasites.
choices.C: Protective software prevents viruses from spreading from one machine to another. Therefore, a network on which every machine has protective software will be free of viruses.
choices.D: Both contagious diseases and rumors spread from one person to another through everyday social contact. Contagious diseases are known to spread much faster in crowded cities than in sparsely populated rural villages. So rumors, too, must spread much faster in crowded cities than in sparsely populated rural villages.
choices.E: Herds in which most animals are vaccinated rarely suffer outbreaks, while herds in which few are vaccinated often do. So vaccinating most of a herd is what prevents outbreaks.

explanations.A: Half right: it is an analogy with the same first case, but it states no mechanism and no respect in which the second case resembles the first, so the transfer is unexplained.
explanations.B: Stimulus: an effect in case one is explained by a mechanism; case two is shown to share the feature that mechanism depends on; the effect is predicted for case two. This choice: crop rotation works because pests specialize; animal parasites also specialize; so rotating livestock should work. Same mechanism-based analogy.
explanations.C: Wrong part: this is a conditional inference about a single domain, with no analogy to a second case.
explanations.D: Half right: an analogy is drawn, but the shared feature (spreading person to person) is not linked to any mechanism that explains the faster spread in cities, so the transfer is not grounded as it is in the stimulus.
explanations.E: Shell game: this infers a cause from a comparison of outcomes within one domain; no second domain and no analogy appear.

keyTakeaway: A strong analogy argument has three parts: an effect, the mechanism behind it, and a second case that shares the mechanism's key feature; the match needs all three.
predictionHint: Effect in X because of mechanism M; Y shares M's key feature; so expect the effect in Y.

stimulus: Some critics maintain that a novel cannot be both commercially successful and formally innovative. But Ilse Varga's novel The Glass Orchard, which abandons conventional chapter structure entirely, sold more copies in its first year than any other novel published that decade. The critics' claim is therefore mistaken.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Some critics say that formally innovative novels rarely sell well. The Glass Orchard was innovative and sold extremely well. So formally innovative novels sell well.
choices.B: Some critics maintain that commercially successful novels are never formally innovative. The Glass Orchard was commercially successful. So, if the critics are right, it was not formally innovative.
choices.C: It is often said that no building can be both energy-efficient and architecturally distinguished. Yet the Marrow Library, which has won three major architectural awards, consumes less energy per square meter than any other public building in the city. So this common view is false.
choices.D: It is often said that no building can be both energy-efficient and architecturally distinguished. The Marrow Library is certainly energy-efficient, consuming less energy per square meter than any other public building in the city. Since it is not architecturally distinguished, however, it does not refute this common view.
choices.E: Critics claim that no novel can be both commercially successful and formally innovative. But most of those critics have never read a formally innovative novel, so their claim should be dismissed.

explanations.A: Opposite: this generalizes from one case to a universal positive claim, an invalid overgeneralization, not a refutation of a 'cannot be both' claim.
explanations.B: Wrong part: this applies the critics' claim as a conditional to one case; it does not refute it.
explanations.C: Stimulus: a claim that nothing is both A and B; an instance that is shown to be both A and B; conclusion that the claim is false. This choice: nothing is both efficient and distinguished; the library is both; the view is false. Same valid refutation by counterexample.
explanations.D: Half right: the same claim and the same building appear, but the case is shown to have only one of the two properties, so it confirms rather than refutes.
explanations.E: Shell game: this dismisses the claim by attacking the critics' experience, an ad hominem, with no counterexample.

keyTakeaway: A valid counterexample to 'nothing is both A and B' must establish both A and B for one case; check that the answer's instance has both properties.
predictionHint: 'No X is both A and B'; here is an X that is A and B; so the claim is false.

stimulus: Whenever the river rises above four meters, the lower road floods, and the ferry cannot operate when the lower road is flooded. The river is forecast to rise above four meters tonight, and such forecasts have proved accurate for this stretch of river. The ferry, therefore, will not operate tonight.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Whenever the river rises above four meters, the lower road floods. The lower road flooded last night. So the river must have risen above four meters last night.
choices.B: The ferry cannot operate when the lower road is flooded, and the lower road floods whenever the river rises above four meters. The ferry did not operate today. So the river rose above four meters today.
choices.C: Whenever the river rises above four meters, the lower road floods, and the ferry cannot operate when the lower road is flooded. The ferry operated on its normal schedule throughout this morning. So the river cannot have risen above four meters this morning.
choices.D: Whenever the factory runs its night shift, the backup generator is in use, and the sawmill cannot draw power while the generator is in use. The factory will run its night shift this week. The sawmill, therefore, will not draw power this week.
choices.E: Whenever the river rises above four meters, the lower road floods. The river rose above four meters tonight. So the lower road will flood tonight.

explanations.A: Opposite: this affirms the consequent of the first conditional, which is invalid.
explanations.B: Shell game: it uses the same chain but runs it backward from the final result to the initial trigger, which is invalid.
explanations.C: Half right: this is a valid contrapositive through the same chain, but it moves from the denial of the final result back to the denial of the trigger; the stimulus moves forward from the trigger to the result.
explanations.D: Stimulus: A leads to B; B rules out C; A will occur; therefore not C. This choice: night shift means generator in use; generator in use rules out sawmill power; night shift will run; therefore no sawmill power. Same forward chain ending in a negative conclusion.
explanations.E: Wrong part: this takes only the first step of the chain and stops at the flooding; the stimulus carries the inference through a second conditional.

keyTakeaway: Match the direction as well as the links: a forward chain (trigger given, result concluded) is not the same as its contrapositive run in reverse.
predictionHint: A → B; B → not C; A; therefore not C.

stimulus: A cargo shipment is subject to inspection only if at least one container in the shipment originates from a country without a customs agreement. Every container in the Marlow shipment originates from a country that has such an agreement. The Marlow shipment, therefore, is not subject to inspection.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: A legislative bill is referred to the finance committee only if at least one of its provisions authorizes spending. None of the provisions of the bill under consideration authorizes spending. The bill, therefore, will not be referred to the finance committee.
choices.B: Under the customs rules, a cargo shipment is subject to inspection if at least one container in the shipment originates from a country without a customs agreement. One of the forty containers in the Dorn shipment originates from such a country. So the Dorn shipment is subject to inspection.
choices.C: A bill is referred to the finance committee only if at least one of its provisions authorizes spending. The bill was referred to the finance committee. So every one of its provisions authorizes spending.
choices.D: A bill is referred to the finance committee only if at least one of its provisions authorizes spending. One provision of the bill authorizes spending. So the bill will be referred to the finance committee.
choices.E: No container in the Marlow shipment originates from a country without a customs agreement. So no container in the Marlow shipment is itself subject to inspection.

explanations.A: Stimulus: the whole has property P only if at least one part has Q; no part has Q; therefore the whole lacks P. This choice: referred only if at least one provision authorizes spending; none does; therefore not referred. Same necessary condition over parts, denied for every part, with the contrapositive drawn for the whole.
explanations.B: Half right: this is valid, but it treats the container condition as sufficient and affirms it; the stimulus treats it as necessary and denies it.
explanations.C: Shell game: it affirms the whole's property and concludes that every part has Q, inflating 'at least one' into 'every.'
explanations.D: Opposite: this affirms the necessary condition and concludes the outcome, which is invalid.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the conclusion is about the containers individually, not about the shipment; the whole-level inference is missing.

keyTakeaway: 'Only if at least one part...' is a necessary condition about parts; denying it for every part validly denies the property for the whole.
predictionHint: Whole is P only if some part is Q; no part is Q; so whole is not P.

stimulus: None of the ceramics produced at the Velk kiln were glazed, since the kiln never reached the temperatures that glazing requires. Some of the ceramics found in the Oris burial mound were glazed. Therefore, some of the ceramics found in the Oris burial mound were not produced at the Velk kiln.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: None of the ceramics produced at the Velk kiln were glazed. Some of the ceramics found at the Oris mound were not glazed. So some of the ceramics found at the Oris mound were produced at the Velk kiln.
choices.B: None of the contracts drafted by the firm's junior associates contain an arbitration clause. Some of the contracts in the Harwood file contain an arbitration clause. Therefore, some of the contracts in the Harwood file were not drafted by the firm's junior associates.
choices.C: No junior associate at the firm drafts contracts containing an arbitration clause, since only partners are authorized to include one. Some of the contracts in the Harwood file were drafted by junior associates. Therefore, some of the contracts in the Harwood file lack an arbitration clause.
choices.D: None of the firm's junior associates drafted the contracts in the Harwood file. Some of the contracts in the Harwood file contain an arbitration clause. So some arbitration clauses were drafted by senior associates.
choices.E: None of the ceramics produced at the Velk kiln were glazed. All of the ceramics found at the Oris mound were glazed. Therefore, none of the ceramics found at the Oris mound were produced at the Velk kiln.

explanations.A: Opposite: from 'no Velk ceramics are glazed' and 'some Oris ceramics are unglazed,' nothing follows about Oris ceramics being from Velk; the inference is invalid.
explanations.B: Stimulus: no A are B; some C are B; therefore some C are not A. This choice: no junior-drafted contracts have the clause; some Harwood contracts have the clause; therefore some Harwood contracts are not junior-drafted. The shared middle term (B, the clause) appears in both premises and drops out, exactly as 'glazed' does.
explanations.C: Half right: this is also a valid syllogism with 'none' and 'some' premises, but the middle term is the junior associates (A), and the conclusion is about lacking B. The stimulus's middle term is B and its conclusion is about not being A.
explanations.D: Shell game: 'senior associates' appears from nowhere; the conclusion introduces a term absent from the premises.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the second premise and the conclusion are universal ('all,' 'none'); the stimulus's 'some' is missing.

keyTakeaway: In no/some syllogisms, identify the middle term that disappears; two valid arguments with the same quantifiers can still differ in which term is shared.
predictionHint: No A are B; some C are B; so some C are not A.

stimulus: If the decline in songbird numbers at the Fenwick reserve were caused by pesticide drift from the nearby farms, songbird numbers at the Alder reserve, which lies equally close to the same farms and downwind of them, would have declined as well. But songbird numbers at Alder have remained stable throughout the period. So pesticide drift is not the cause of the decline at Fenwick.
stem: The pattern of reasoning in which one of the following is most similar to that in the argument above?

choices.A: Songbird numbers at Fenwick declined after the nearby farms began spraying pesticide, while numbers at Alder, which lies far from any farm, remained stable. So pesticide drift caused the decline at Fenwick.
choices.B: If pesticide drift caused the decline at Fenwick, the songbirds there would show pesticide residues in their tissues. They do show such residues. So pesticide drift caused the decline.
choices.C: If the new shift schedule caused the rise in absenteeism at the Lorne factory, absenteeism would have risen at the Corbett factory as well. It did rise at Corbett. So the schedule is probably the cause of the rise at Lorne.
choices.D: If the new shift schedule had caused the rise in absenteeism at the Lorne factory, absenteeism there would have risen soon after the schedule changed. In fact, it did not begin to rise until a full year after the change. So the new shift schedule is not the cause of the rise in absenteeism.
choices.E: If the rise in absenteeism at the Lorne factory were due to the new shift schedule, absenteeism at the Corbett factory, which adopted the identical schedule at the same time, would have risen as well. But absenteeism at Corbett is unchanged. So the new schedule is not the cause of the rise at Lorne.

explanations.A: Shell game: this uses a comparison case to confirm a causal hypothesis rather than to refute one; the direction of the inference is reversed.
explanations.B: Opposite: this affirms the consequent of the prediction, an invalid confirmation.
explanations.C: Wrong force: the prediction is confirmed rather than disconfirmed, and the conclusion is a hedged 'probably'; the stimulus refutes.
explanations.D: Half right: the logical form (if H, then P; not P; so not H) matches, but the prediction concerns timing within the same case, not a comparison case exposed to the same supposed cause. The stimulus's method depends on the similarly situated second site.
explanations.E: Stimulus: if the hypothesis were true, a comparably exposed second case would show the same effect; it does not; so the hypothesis is false. This choice: if the schedule were the cause, Corbett, with the identical schedule, would show the rise; it does not; so the schedule is not the cause. Same test of a causal claim against a matched case.

keyTakeaway: When a causal hypothesis is refuted by a matched comparison case, the match needs both the modus tollens form and a second case exposed to the same supposed cause.
predictionHint: If cause, then matched case would show effect; it doesn't; so not the cause.

stimulus:
Marketing director: We should move all of our customer service to an automated chat system. It would answer most questions instantly and cut our service costs by a third.

Operations manager: The savings are real. But our customers are mostly older people who have told us repeatedly that they want to speak with a person. Automating customer service would drive many of them to our competitors.
stem: The dialogue most supports the claim that the marketing director and the operations manager disagree about whether

choices.A: an automated chat system would reduce the company's customer service costs
choices.B: the company's customers are mostly older people
choices.C: the company should move all of its customer service to an automated chat system
choices.D: an automated chat system could answer most customer questions instantly
choices.E: cost savings matter more to the company than its customers' preferences do

explanations.A: Opposite: the manager says 'The savings are real,' so both accept this.
explanations.B: Out of scope: only the manager mentions the customers' ages; the director takes no position.
explanations.C: The director says 'We should move'; the manager argues the move would drive customers away. One recommends, the other opposes.
explanations.D: Out of scope: only the director makes this claim, and the manager neither affirms nor denies it.
explanations.E: Shell game: neither speaker ranks savings against preferences in general; the manager's point is about losing customers, not about which value matters more.

keyTakeaway: The point at issue is usually the first speaker's recommendation; confirm that the second speaker actually argues against it.
predictionHint: Whether to automate customer service.

stimulus:
Teacher: Students should memorize key dates in history. Without a fixed chronology in mind, they cannot see how events influenced one another.

Principal: Memorized dates are forgotten within months, as every test we have given shows. Students come to see how events influenced one another when they study the causes of those events, not when they memorize when the events happened.
stem: The teacher and the principal disagree over whether

choices.A: memorizing key dates helps students understand how historical events influenced one another
choices.B: students should study the causes of historical events
choices.C: students forget memorized dates within months
choices.D: understanding how historical events influenced one another is an important goal of history instruction
choices.E: history tests should ask students to recall dates

explanations.A: The teacher says memorizing dates is needed to see how events influenced one another; the principal says that understanding comes from studying causes, 'not when they memorize.' They disagree about whether memorization helps.
explanations.B: Out of scope: only the principal mentions studying causes, and the teacher does not oppose it.
explanations.C: Out of scope: only the principal claims this; the teacher says nothing about retention.
explanations.D: Opposite: both treat this understanding as the goal; they differ only over how to reach it.
explanations.E: Shell game: the principal mentions tests as evidence about forgetting, but neither speaker says what tests should ask.

keyTakeaway: When both speakers share a goal, the point at issue is the means: does the first speaker's method actually achieve it?
predictionHint: Whether memorizing dates helps students understand historical influence.

stimulus:
Researcher: The new screening test detects the disease at an earlier stage than the standard test does, so hospitals should adopt it. Earlier detection allows earlier treatment.

Physician: Earlier detection does allow earlier treatment. But for this disease, no treatment begun early has been shown to improve outcomes over treatment begun at the stage the standard test detects. Adopting the new test would only lengthen the period during which patients know they are ill.
stem: The dialogue most supports the claim that the researcher and the physician disagree about whether

choices.A: the new screening test detects the disease at an earlier stage than the standard test does
choices.B: patients prefer to learn of their illness as early as possible
choices.C: the standard screening test should continue to be used alongside the new test
choices.D: hospitals should adopt the new screening test
choices.E: the cost of adopting the new test outweighs its benefits

explanations.A: Opposite: the physician does not dispute earlier detection; the objection concerns what earlier detection accomplishes.
explanations.B: Out of scope: neither speaker reports what patients prefer; the physician describes a consequence, not a preference.
explanations.C: Out of scope: neither speaker discusses using the two tests together.
explanations.D: The researcher concludes 'hospitals should adopt it'; the physician argues adoption would only lengthen the period of worry, opposing adoption. This is the point of disagreement.
explanations.E: Shell game: no one mentions cost; the physician's objection is about outcomes, not expense.

keyTakeaway: A second speaker who concedes the premises ('does allow') and attacks the conclusion disagrees about the recommendation, not the facts.
predictionHint: Whether hospitals should adopt the new test.

stimulus:
Prosecutor: Plea bargains should be abolished. They allow the guilty to receive sentences far lighter than their crimes warrant.

Defense attorney: Plea bargains do result in lighter sentences. Yet without them the courts would be so backlogged that defendants would wait years for trial, and many innocent people would plead guilty simply to end their detention. Plea bargains are the lesser evil.
stem: The prosecutor and the defense attorney disagree over whether

choices.A: plea bargains result in lighter sentences for defendants than they would otherwise receive
choices.B: plea bargains should be abolished entirely
choices.C: abolishing plea bargains would increase the backlog in the courts
choices.D: innocent defendants sometimes plead guilty in order to end their detention
choices.E: the primary purpose of sentencing is to punish the guilty in proportion to their crimes

explanations.A: Opposite: the attorney says 'Plea bargains do result in lighter sentences,' agreeing with the prosecutor on this.
explanations.B: The prosecutor's first sentence calls for abolition; the attorney argues that the alternative is worse and that plea bargains are 'the lesser evil,' which is a case against abolition.
explanations.C: Out of scope: only the attorney discusses backlogs; the prosecutor expresses no view.
explanations.D: Out of scope: only the attorney raises innocent defendants' pleas.
explanations.E: Shell game: the prosecutor's complaint about light sentences hints at proportionality, but neither speaker states what sentencing's primary purpose is.

keyTakeaway: 'The lesser evil' is a verdict that the thing should be kept; it puts the speaker in direct opposition to a call for abolition.
predictionHint: Whether plea bargains should be abolished.

stimulus:

Conservator: Without the reconstructed panels, visitors cannot grasp the fresco's composition at all; they would see only disconnected fragments. Since the reconstruction is clearly marked as modern work, displaying it deceives no one.
stem: The dialogue most supports the claim that the curator and the conservator disagree about whether

choices.A: the reconstruction of the missing panels is clearly marked as modern work
choices.B: visitors to the gallery deserve to see what has survived of the fresco
choices.C: most visitors to the gallery are capable of appreciating fragmentary works of art
choices.D: some of the fresco's original panels are missing
choices.E: the gallery should display the fresco together with the modern reconstruction of its missing panels

explanations.A: Out of scope: only the conservator says this; the curator does not dispute the labeling.
explanations.B: Out of scope: only the curator asserts this, and the conservator does not deny it; the conservator's point is about comprehension, not desert.
explanations.C: Shell game: the conservator says visitors cannot grasp the composition from fragments, which is about what the fragments show, not about visitors' capacities in general. Neither speaker addresses this.
explanations.D: Opposite: both speakers presuppose that panels are missing; the dispute is over what to do about it.
explanations.E: The curator wants the fresco shown 'without the modern reconstruction'; the conservator argues the reconstruction is needed and harmless. They disagree about displaying it.

keyTakeaway: Each speaker's reasons may go unchallenged; the disagreement lives in the recommendations those reasons support.
predictionHint: Whether to display the reconstruction with the fresco.

stimulus:
Economist: Rent control keeps housing affordable for the tenants who already have it, but it discourages construction of new rental housing, so it ultimately reduces the supply of affordable homes. Cities should abandon it.

Housing advocate: Construction does slow under rent control. But the tenants it protects would otherwise be displaced immediately, whereas new construction takes years to help anyone. Cities should keep rent control until enough housing has been built.
stem: The economist and the housing advocate disagree over whether

choices.A: cities should abandon rent control at present
choices.B: rent control discourages the construction of new rental housing
choices.C: new construction takes years to benefit tenants
choices.D: rent control reduces the long-run supply of affordable housing
choices.E: protecting current tenants is more important than increasing the housing supply

explanations.A: The economist says cities 'should abandon' rent control; the advocate says they 'should keep' it until more housing exists. They disagree about abandoning it now.
explanations.B: Opposite: the advocate concedes 'Construction does slow under rent control.'
explanations.C: Out of scope: only the advocate makes this claim; the economist does not address it.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the economist asserts this, but the advocate concedes only that construction slows and takes no position on long-run supply. A claim one speaker leaves open cannot be the point at issue.
explanations.E: Shell game: the advocate's position suggests a priority, but neither speaker states a general ranking of these goals; the advocate's claim is about timing, not importance.

keyTakeaway: Conceding a mechanism ('construction does slow') is not conceding the conclusion drawn from it; check what the second speaker actually commits to.
predictionHint: Whether to abandon rent control now.

stimulus:
Linguist: Children acquire the grammar of their first language without explicit instruction, and they do so in a fixed sequence regardless of which language they learn. This shows that the basic structure of grammar is innate.

Psychologist: The sequence is indeed fixed across languages. But the same sequence appears when adults learn an artificial language in the laboratory, and adults do not rely on an innate grammar to do so. The fixed sequence reflects general constraints on learning, not knowledge of grammar present at birth.
stem: The dialogue most supports the claim that the linguist and the psychologist disagree about whether

choices.A: children acquire grammar in a fixed sequence regardless of the language they learn
choices.B: adults learning an artificial language acquire its grammar in the same sequence as children acquiring a first language
choices.C: the fixed order in which children acquire grammar shows that grammatical structure is innate
choices.D: children receive explicit instruction in the grammar of their first language
choices.E: general constraints on learning play some role in how children acquire grammar

explanations.A: Opposite: the psychologist says 'The sequence is indeed fixed across languages.'
explanations.B: Out of scope: only the psychologist reports the adult finding; the linguist takes no position on it.
explanations.C: The linguist says the fixed sequence 'shows that' grammar is innate; the psychologist says it reflects general learning constraints, 'not knowledge of grammar present at birth.' They disagree about what the sequence shows.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the linguist denies this; the psychologist never addresses instruction.
explanations.E: Shell game: the psychologist affirms this, but the linguist does not deny that learning constraints play 'some role'; the linguist's claim is about what the sequence demonstrates.

keyTakeaway: When speakers agree on the data, the point at issue is the inference: what the shared evidence shows.
predictionHint: Whether the fixed sequence is evidence of innate grammar.

stimulus:
Archaeologist: The copper ornaments found in the Lesk burials were made of ore from mines four hundred kilometers away. The Lesk people therefore traded over long distances.

Anthropologist: The ore's origin is not in doubt. But ornaments pass from hand to hand through many short exchanges between neighboring groups, each of which may never have traveled more than a day's walk. The ornaments' origin tells us nothing about how far the Lesk people themselves traveled or traded.
stem: The archaeologist and the anthropologist disagree over whether

choices.A: the copper in the Lesk ornaments came from mines four hundred kilometers away
choices.B: ornaments typically passed between neighboring groups through many short exchanges
choices.C: the Lesk people traded over long distances
choices.D: the origin of the ore in the Lesk ornaments is evidence that the Lesk people traded over long distances
choices.E: the Lesk people obtained the ornaments from a neighboring group

explanations.A: Opposite: the anthropologist says 'The ore's origin is not in doubt.'
explanations.B: Out of scope: only the anthropologist describes this mechanism; the archaeologist does not address it.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the archaeologist asserts this, but the anthropologist says only that the ornaments' origin 'tells us nothing' about it, taking no position on whether the Lesk people did trade over long distances. One speaker is silent on the truth of the claim itself.
explanations.D: The archaeologist infers long-distance trade from the ore's origin ('therefore'); the anthropologist says the origin 'tells us nothing' about that. They disagree about the evidential link.
explanations.E: Shell game: the anthropologist offers hand-to-hand exchange as a possibility that undercuts the inference, not as a claim about what actually happened, and the archaeologist does not address it.

keyTakeaway: 'Tells us nothing about X' disputes the inference to X, not X itself; the disagreement is about whether the evidence supports the claim.
predictionHint: Whether the ore's origin supports the long-distance trade inference.

stimulus:
Ethicist: A company that discovers a safety defect in its product is obligated to notify customers immediately, even before it has determined how serious the defect is. Customers can then decide for themselves what risk to accept.

Executive: Customers cannot evaluate a risk the company itself has not yet measured. Notifying them before the defect is understood produces panic rather than informed choice. The obligation to notify arises only once the company can tell customers what the defect means for them.
stem: The dialogue most supports the claim that the ethicist and the executive disagree about whether

choices.A: companies have some obligation to notify customers of safety defects in their products
choices.B: a company that discovers a safety defect is obligated to notify customers before it has determined how serious the defect is
choices.C: customers would panic if notified of a defect before its seriousness is known
choices.D: customers are entitled to decide for themselves what risks to accept
choices.E: companies should determine the seriousness of a defect as quickly as possible

explanations.A: Opposite: both speakers accept an obligation to notify; they differ only about when it begins.
explanations.B: The ethicist says the obligation applies 'immediately, even before' seriousness is known; the executive says it 'arises only once' the company can explain the defect. They disagree about notification before the defect is understood.
explanations.C: Out of scope: only the executive predicts panic; the ethicist does not address it.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the ethicist asserts this; the executive says customers cannot evaluate an unmeasured risk, which concerns their ability, not their entitlement, and takes no stand on entitlement.
explanations.E: Shell game: neither speaker says how quickly a company should investigate; both discuss when to notify, not when to measure.

keyTakeaway: 'Only once' versus 'even before' marks a disagreement about timing; the right answer must include the timing condition, not just the obligation.
predictionHint: Whether the duty to notify begins before the defect's seriousness is known.

stimulus:
City planner: The proposed bicycle lanes on Grand Avenue will reduce the number of cars on the avenue, since surveys show that many residents would cycle if a protected lane existed. The lanes should be built.

Merchant: Surveys of what people say they would do are a poor guide to what they actually do. But the lanes would at least slow the traffic that remains, which is what the avenue's pedestrians most need. Build them, by all means.
stem: The city planner and the merchant are committed to agreeing about which one of the following?

choices.A: The bicycle lanes would reduce the number of cars on Grand Avenue.
choices.B: Surveys of what people say they would do are a poor guide to their actual behavior.
choices.C: The bicycle lanes should not be built unless surveys reliably predict residents' behavior.
choices.D: The bicycle lanes on Grand Avenue should be built.
choices.E: Reducing traffic is the main purpose of the proposed bicycle lanes.

explanations.A: Out of scope: the planner asserts this, but the merchant doubts the survey evidence for it and never affirms it.
explanations.B: Out of scope: only the merchant makes this claim.
explanations.C: Opposite: both speakers want the lanes built, and the merchant supports them despite doubting the surveys.
explanations.D: The planner says 'The lanes should be built'; the merchant says 'Build them, by all means.' Different reasons, same recommendation.
explanations.E: Shell game: the planner cites traffic reduction as a benefit, and the merchant cites pedestrian safety; neither says what the 'main purpose' is.

keyTakeaway: Speakers can agree on a recommendation while disputing each other's reasons; in agreement questions, look at the conclusions first.
predictionHint: Both say: build the lanes.

stimulus:
Critic: Abridged editions of classic novels should not be published. Readers who finish an abridgment believe they have read the novel, when in fact they have read an editor's summary of it.

Publisher: Readers of abridgments do often mistake them for the originals, and that is regrettable. But most of those readers would never attempt the full novel, and an abridgment at least acquaints them with its characters and plot. Better that than nothing.
stem: The critic and the publisher are committed to agreeing about which one of the following?

choices.A: Readers of abridged editions often mistakenly believe they have read the original novel.
choices.B: Abridged editions of classic novels should not be published.
choices.C: Most readers of abridgments would not attempt the full novel.
choices.D: Acquainting readers with a novel's characters and plot is worthwhile even if they never read the novel.
choices.E: Abridged editions should carry a prominent notice stating that they are abridged.

explanations.A: The critic asserts it; the publisher says 'Readers of abridgments do often mistake them for the originals.' Both are committed to it.
explanations.B: Opposite: this is the point of disagreement; the publisher defends abridgments.
explanations.C: Out of scope: only the publisher claims this.
explanations.D: Out of scope: only the publisher takes this position; the critic does not address it.
explanations.E: Shell game: a notice is a plausible remedy, but neither speaker proposes or discusses one.

keyTakeaway: The second speaker's concession ('do often... and that is regrettable') is the point of agreement; everything after 'But' is contested or one-sided.
predictionHint: Both accept that readers mistake abridgments for the real thing.

stimulus:
Geologist: The tremors recorded near the Avon reservoir since it was filled are caused by the weight of the impounded water, which has increased pressure on a fault beneath the reservoir. The reservoir should be partly drained.

Engineer: Draining the reservoir would not stop the tremors; once pressure on a fault has shifted, the fault continues to adjust for years. The tremors are too small to damage the dam, and the reservoir supplies the region's water. It should remain full.
stem: The geologist and the engineer are committed to agreeing about which one of the following?

choices.A: The reservoir should be partly drained.
choices.B: The tremors near the reservoir are too small to damage the dam.
choices.C: The filling of the reservoir has altered the pressure on a fault beneath it.
choices.D: The tremors would continue for years even if the reservoir were drained.
choices.E: The region's need for water outweighs any risk posed by the tremors.

explanations.A: Opposite: the engineer says the reservoir 'should remain full.'
explanations.B: Out of scope: only the engineer assesses the danger to the dam.
explanations.C: The geologist says the water 'has increased pressure on a fault'; the engineer's reply presupposes it: 'once pressure on a fault has shifted.' Both are committed to the pressure change.
explanations.D: Out of scope: only the engineer makes this prediction; the geologist, who recommends draining, implicitly expects it to help.
explanations.E: Shell game: the engineer weighs water supply against small tremors, but the geologist offers no such comparison, and 'any risk' goes beyond what even the engineer says.

keyTakeaway: A reply that begins 'once X has happened' presupposes X; presuppositions count as commitments in agreement questions.
predictionHint: Both accept that the reservoir changed pressure on the fault.

stimulus:
Dean: The university should stop requiring students to buy printed textbooks. Free online materials now cover every introductory course at least as well as the textbooks do, and students can ill afford the expense.

Professor: Online materials are frequently revised without notice, so a student and an instructor may find themselves reading different versions. Printed textbooks have the stability a course needs. The expense, though, is a real burden, and the university ought to subsidize it.
stem: The dean and the professor are committed to agreeing about which one of the following?

choices.A: Free online materials cover introductory courses at least as well as printed textbooks do.
choices.B: The university should stop requiring students to buy printed textbooks.
choices.C: Online materials are frequently revised without notice.
choices.D: Students should not be required to spend money on any course materials.
choices.E: The cost of printed textbooks is a significant burden on students.

explanations.A: Out of scope: the dean asserts this; the professor objects to online materials on other grounds and never affirms their coverage.
explanations.B: Opposite: the professor wants textbooks kept and the cost subsidized, which is a rejection of the dean's proposal.
explanations.C: Out of scope: only the professor makes this claim.
explanations.D: Extreme: the dean objects to the textbook expense specifically, and the professor wants it subsidized; neither says students should pay for no materials at all.
explanations.E: The dean says students 'can ill afford the expense'; the professor says 'The expense, though, is a real burden.' Both are committed to the cost being a significant burden.

keyTakeaway: The word 'though' in the second speaker's final sentence often introduces the one concession to the first speaker, which is the point of agreement.
predictionHint: Both agree textbooks cost students too much.

stimulus: Physician: Patients who take the new blood-pressure medication once daily must take it at the same time each day, since its effectiveness drops sharply if successive doses are more than two hours apart in timing. Many of my patients work irregular shifts and cannot reliably take anything at the same time each day. For those patients, then, ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: the new medication should be taken twice daily rather than once
choices.B: the new medication is unlikely to be fully effective
choices.C: no blood-pressure medication will be effective
choices.D: irregular work schedules are the main cause of their high blood pressure
choices.E: the new medication will be fully effective provided they take it every day

explanations.A: Out of scope: nothing in the premises addresses twice-daily dosing or its effects.
explanations.B: Effectiveness requires consistent timing; these patients cannot time doses consistently; so for them the drug is unlikely to be fully effective. The conclusion follows directly and is appropriately hedged.
explanations.C: Extreme: the premises concern only this medication; 'no blood-pressure medication' generalizes beyond them.
explanations.D: Shell game: the passage is about when doses are taken, not about what causes high blood pressure.
explanations.E: Opposite: the premises say taking it daily is not enough; timing matters, and these patients cannot keep the timing.

keyTakeaway: Combine the conditional requirement with the fact that the group cannot meet it, and conclude only about that group and that drug.
predictionHint: The drug probably won't work well for them.

stimulus: The Larkin Bakery has decided to stop selling its bread through supermarkets and to sell only at its own shop. The decision makes sense. Supermarkets pay the bakery barely more than the cost of ingredients, whereas customers at the shop pay nearly twice that. And the bakery can expect to sell about as much bread at the shop as it now sells altogether, since ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: the bakery's shop is located in a neighborhood that already has several other bakeries
choices.B: supermarkets have been selling Larkin bread for less than the bakery charges at its shop
choices.C: the bakery's bread is of higher quality than the bread sold by most supermarkets
choices.D: the bakery would save on delivery costs by selling only at its own shop
choices.E: most of the customers who now buy Larkin bread at supermarkets have said they would buy it at the shop instead

explanations.A: Opposite: nearby competition would make it harder, not easier, to keep the same volume.
explanations.B: Premise booster: this restates the price gap already given; it says nothing about whether supermarket customers will follow the bread to the shop.
explanations.C: Out of scope: quality does not explain why current supermarket buyers would travel to the shop.
explanations.D: Shell game: delivery savings would strengthen the cost side of the decision, but the blank must support the claim about sales volume.
explanations.E: The blank must explain why shop sales will match current total sales. If most supermarket customers will switch to the shop, the volume follows.

keyTakeaway: When the blank follows 'since,' it must support the specific claim immediately before it, not the argument's overall conclusion.
predictionHint: A reason supermarket buyers will come to the shop.

stimulus: Juror anonymity is justified when jurors face a genuine risk of intimidation. But anonymity also prevents the public from knowing whether the jury was properly selected, and that knowledge is essential to confidence in verdicts. So anonymity should be granted only when the risk of intimidation is serious and specific. In the Dorsey trial, the only basis for the prosecution's request for anonymity is that the case has drawn extensive press coverage. It follows that ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: the prosecution's request for juror anonymity in the Dorsey trial should be denied
choices.B: the Dorsey trial should be moved to a location where it has received less press coverage
choices.C: jurors in the Dorsey trial face no risk of intimidation whatsoever
choices.D: press coverage of the Dorsey trial will undermine public confidence in the verdict
choices.E: the prosecution's request should be granted because press coverage increases the risk of intimidation

explanations.A: The rule is 'anonymity only when the risk is serious and specific.' The Dorsey request rests only on press coverage, which is neither. Applying the rule, the request should be denied.
explanations.B: Out of scope: a change of venue is never discussed; the argument concerns anonymity.
explanations.C: Extreme: the argument shows the risk is not 'serious and specific'; 'no risk whatsoever' claims more than the premises support.
explanations.D: Shell game: it is anonymity, not press coverage, that the passage says undermines confidence.
explanations.E: Opposite: the argument treats press coverage as an insufficient basis; this completion grants the request on that very basis.

keyTakeaway: A rule stated with 'only when' plus a case that fails the condition yields a denial; the completion should apply the rule, not restate the risk.
predictionHint: Deny the request.

stimulus: Ecologist: The island's population of ground-nesting seabirds has fallen by half since rats arrived on cargo ships a decade ago, and the rats are certainly responsible: they eat eggs and chicks. Some have proposed introducing cats to control the rats. But even if the cats eliminated every rat on the island, the seabirds would be no better off, since ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: cats introduced to other islands have sometimes failed to reduce rat populations
choices.B: rats reached the island on cargo ships that continue to call there regularly
choices.C: the seabird population was already declining slowly before the rats arrived
choices.D: cats prey on ground-nesting seabirds and their eggs at least as readily as rats do
choices.E: the cats would eventually eliminate the rats entirely

explanations.A: Wrong force: 'sometimes failed' is too weak, and the sentence concedes the cats succeed against rats; what is needed is a reason the birds still suffer.
explanations.B: True but irrelevant: continued ship traffic bears on reinfestation, but the argument stipulates the rats are gone.
explanations.C: Out of scope: a slow prior decline does not show the birds would be 'no better off' after the main threat is removed.
explanations.D: The blank must explain why removing the rats leaves the birds no better off. If the cats themselves prey on the birds as readily, one predator replaces another, and the birds gain nothing.
explanations.E: Opposite: this restates the concession ('even if the cats eliminated every rat') and offers no reason the birds would fail to benefit.

keyTakeaway: An 'even if X, still Y, since ____' blank needs a reason Y holds despite X; look for the substitute problem, not a reason X might fail.
predictionHint: The cats would hurt the birds just as much.

stimulus: Economist: The government claims that its job-training program lifted participants' earnings, noting that participants earned twenty percent more two years after the program than they had before it. But the program enrolled only people who had recently lost their jobs, and most people who lose a job see their earnings recover substantially within two years whether or not they receive training. Thus, the government's figures ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: show that the program had no effect on participants' earnings
choices.B: would have been more convincing had the program enrolled people who were already employed
choices.C: do not by themselves show that the program raised participants' earnings
choices.D: overstate the percentage by which participants' earnings actually rose
choices.E: prove that participants would have recovered their earnings without the program

explanations.A: Extreme: the alternative explanation undercuts the government's inference; it does not establish that the program did nothing.
explanations.B: Shell game: the problem is the absence of a comparison group, not the employment status of enrollees; enrolling the employed would not address recovery effects.
explanations.C: Earnings typically recover after job loss regardless of training, so the twenty percent rise is consistent with the program having done nothing. The figures therefore fail to establish the causal claim.
explanations.D: Out of scope: the economist never disputes the figures' accuracy, only what they show.
explanations.E: Opposite: 'prove' and 'would have recovered' assert the alternative as fact; the economist shows only that it cannot be ruled out.

keyTakeaway: An alternative explanation licenses 'the evidence does not show X,' never 'X is false'; keep the completion at the evidential level.
predictionHint: The numbers don't establish the program caused the gain.

stimulus: Art critic: A forgery that is indistinguishable from an original, even to experts, is nonetheless worth less than the original, and rightly so. Some say this shows that collectors value the artist's name rather than the work itself. But the value of a work of art depends partly on the achievement it represents, and a forger who copies an existing work achieves far less than the artist who first conceived it. The lower value of the forgery, then, need not reflect mere name-worship, provided that ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: experts can eventually learn to distinguish the forgery from the original
choices.B: valuing a work for the achievement it represents is not the same as valuing it for its creator's name
choices.C: the forger's technical skill is inferior to that of the original artist
choices.D: collectors are always able to tell which works represent genuine achievements
choices.E: the forgery is worth as much as the original to anyone who cannot tell them apart

explanations.A: Out of scope: the argument stipulates indistinguishability; whether that changes later is irrelevant to the value question.
explanations.B: The critic's defense works only if achievement-based value is a different thing from name-based value. The 'provided that' blank must supply exactly that distinction; without it, the opponent could say valuing achievement just is valuing the name.
explanations.C: Shell game: the passage says the forgery is indistinguishable, so skill is not the difference; the critic locates the difference in conception ('first conceived'), not technique.
explanations.D: Extreme: 'always' is unnecessary and unsupported; the argument needs only that achievement can be a legitimate basis of value.
explanations.E: Opposite: this concedes equal worth to the forgery, contradicting the critic's premise that it is 'rightly' worth less.

keyTakeaway: A 'provided that' blank asks for the condition the argument needs; find the gap between the author's reason and the opponent's charge.
predictionHint: Achievement-value is distinct from name-value.

stimulus: Historian: Almost every surviving letter from the Verrin monastery complains of shortages of parchment. Some scholars infer from this that the monastery was impoverished. But letters were written precisely when something needed to be requested, and parchment was the one thing a monastery could not produce for itself. A well-supplied monastery would have had little occasion to write letters at all. The surviving letters therefore ____.
stem: Which one of the following most logically completes the argument?

choices.A: provide little evidence that the monastery was impoverished
choices.B: show that the monastery was in fact prosperous
choices.C: were written mainly to other monasteries that had surplus parchment
choices.D: are unrepresentative of the monastery's correspondence as a whole
choices.E: prove that parchment was scarce throughout the region

explanations.A: The letters exist because requests were needed, and parchment was what any monastery had to request. So complaints about parchment are expected from any monastery, poor or not, and the letters tell us little about wealth.
explanations.B: Opposite: undermining the inference to poverty does not establish prosperity; the historian claims only that the evidence is uninformative.
explanations.C: Out of scope: the recipients of the letters are never discussed.
explanations.D: Shell game: the historian's point is that letters are a biased window on monastery life, not that the surviving letters misrepresent the correspondence; nothing suggests other letters differed.
explanations.E: Extreme: the argument concerns one monastery's reasons for writing, not regional supply, and 'prove' overreaches.

keyTakeaway: When an author explains why evidence would look the same either way, the completion is that the evidence is weak, not that the opposite conclusion holds.
predictionHint: The letters are weak evidence of poverty.

stimulus: Mayor: Opponents of the new recycling program say that it is too expensive. But the program costs each household less than the price of one cup of coffee per month, and it diverts a third of the city's waste from the landfill, whose expansion would cost the city far more than the program does. The program is well worth its cost.
stem: The mayor's argument proceeds by

choices.A: questioning the sincerity of the program's opponents
choices.B: denying that the program imposes any cost on households
choices.C: showing that the cost of the program is small compared with the cost of the alternative it avoids
choices.D: pointing out that the opponents' estimate of the program's cost is inaccurate
choices.E: appealing to the environmental benefits of recycling

explanations.A: Out of scope: the mayor says nothing about the opponents' motives.
explanations.B: Opposite: the mayor concedes a cost ('less than the price of one cup of coffee') rather than denying one.
explanations.C: The mayor sets the program's small cost against the much larger cost of expanding the landfill, which the program avoids. That comparison is the whole argument.
explanations.D: Shell game: no estimate by the opponents is mentioned or disputed; the mayor accepts the cost and argues it is worthwhile.
explanations.E: Wrong part: diverting waste is mentioned, but only as the means of avoiding the landfill's expense; no environmental benefit is invoked.

keyTakeaway: When an author grants a cost and names a larger cost it prevents, the method is cost comparison, not denial.
predictionHint: Compares the cost to the cost of the alternative.

stimulus: Columnist: Some claim that people are happiest when they have as many choices as possible. But in one study, shoppers offered twenty varieties of tea were less likely to buy any at all, and less satisfied with what they did buy, than shoppers offered only five varieties. So an abundance of choice does not necessarily make people happier.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the technique of reasoning used in the columnist's argument?

choices.A: showing that the claim being disputed is internally inconsistent
choices.B: arguing that those who make the claim have a financial interest in its acceptance
choices.C: proposing an alternative explanation for a finding cited by proponents of the claim
choices.D: citing an experimental result that conflicts with the claim being disputed
choices.E: demonstrating that having fewer choices always makes people happier

explanations.A: Shell game: the claim is contradicted by outside evidence, not shown to contradict itself.
explanations.B: Out of scope: no one's motives or interests are discussed.
explanations.C: Opposite: the proponents cite no finding; it is the columnist who introduces the study.
explanations.D: The columnist reports a study whose outcome runs against the claim that more choice means more happiness, and concludes the claim does not hold generally. That is refutation by conflicting evidence.
explanations.E: Extreme: 'always' overstates a conclusion phrased as 'does not necessarily.'

keyTakeaway: A single study used against a general claim is 'evidence that conflicts with the claim'; the modest conclusion ('not necessarily') confirms the method.
predictionHint: Uses a study result to undercut a general claim.

stimulus: Attorney: The defendant's fingerprints were on the window, but that does not show he broke in. He had visited the house as a guest two days before the burglary and, by the owner's own account, had opened that very window to let in some air. The fingerprints are exactly what we would expect to find if he is innocent.
stem: The attorney's argument proceeds by

choices.A: disputing the accuracy of the fingerprint evidence
choices.B: attacking the credibility of the homeowner's testimony
choices.C: presenting an alibi that places the defendant elsewhere at the time of the burglary
choices.D: demonstrating that the defendant had no motive to commit the burglary
choices.E: arguing that the evidence cited is just as consistent with the defendant's innocence as with his guilt

explanations.A: Opposite: the attorney accepts that the prints are the defendant's and explains them.
explanations.B: Out of scope: the attorney relies on the owner's account rather than attacking it.
explanations.C: Shell game: the guest visit was two days before the burglary, not at the time of it; it is not an alibi.
explanations.D: Out of scope: motive is never mentioned.
explanations.E: The attorney offers an innocent explanation for the prints and concludes they are 'exactly what we would expect' if he is innocent. The evidence therefore fails to discriminate between guilt and innocence.

keyTakeaway: 'Exactly what we would expect if X' signals the method of showing evidence is equally consistent with a rival hypothesis.
predictionHint: Shows the evidence fits innocence as well as guilt.

stimulus: Economist: Critics of the proposed tax credit argue that it will mainly benefit wealthy households, since wealthy households buy most of the new electric vehicles that qualify for it. But the credit will lower the price of used electric vehicles too, because more new ones will be sold and later resold, and used vehicles are bought disproportionately by households of modest means. The critics have overlooked an important effect of the credit.
stem: The economist's argument proceeds by

choices.A: identifying an indirect effect of the proposal that undermines the critics' objection
choices.B: denying the critics' claim that wealthy households buy most of the qualifying vehicles
choices.C: arguing that the critics' objection, even if correct, is irrelevant to whether the credit should be adopted
choices.D: showing that the critics' objection rests on an ambiguous use of the term 'benefit'
choices.E: questioning the critics' motives for opposing the credit

explanations.B: Opposite: the economist does not dispute who buys new vehicles; the response works around that fact.

stimulus: Historian: Some have inferred from the absence of coins at the Thal settlement that its inhabitants did not use money. But an absence of this kind proves little. Coins were valuable and portable, and people leaving a settlement take their valuables with them. The inhabitants of the nearby Orrin settlement certainly used money, as their written records show, yet excavations there have turned up only two coins.
stem: The historian's argument proceeds by

choices.A: presenting direct evidence that the inhabitants of Thal used money
choices.B: citing a case in which the evidence relied on by the inference is present but the conclusion drawn from it is false
choices.C: showing that the inference rests on an assumption that the inhabitants of Thal and Orrin had similar customs
choices.D: arguing that the inhabitants of Thal deliberately removed evidence of their use of money
choices.E: demonstrating that the absence of coins at Thal is better explained by the settlement's poverty

explanations.A: Opposite: the historian offers no evidence about Thal's use of money, only reasons the absence of coins is uninformative.
explanations.B: At Orrin, coins are nearly absent (the same evidence) yet money was certainly used (the conclusion 'did not use money' would be false). This counterexample shows the inference pattern is unreliable.
explanations.C: Shell game: the historian uses Orrin as a counterexample, not as a premise about shared customs; no such assumption is attributed to the inference.
explanations.D: Extreme: the historian says people take valuables when they leave, a general tendency; 'deliberately removed evidence' adds an intention never claimed.
explanations.E: Out of scope: poverty is never mentioned, and the historian offers no competing explanation specific to Thal.

keyTakeaway: A comparison case where the same evidence appears but the inferred conclusion is known to be false is a counterexample to the inference, not evidence about the original case.
predictionHint: Undermines the inference with a case where it would fail.

stimulus: Philosopher: Some argue that because we cannot be certain of anything beyond our own immediate experience, we should withhold belief about the external world. But if we followed this advice consistently, we would have to withhold belief that other people exist, that the past occurred, and that our next breath will not be our last. Since no one can actually live in that way, the advice must be rejected.
stem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the technique of reasoning used in the philosopher's argument?

choices.A: demonstrating that certainty about the external world is in fact attainable
choices.B: arguing that the recommendation is based on a false premise about the limits of knowledge
choices.C: showing that a recommendation, if followed consistently, would lead to consequences that are unacceptable
choices.D: pointing out that those who make the recommendation do not follow it themselves
choices.E: offering an alternative account of how beliefs about the external world are justified

explanations.A: Opposite: the philosopher never disputes the premise that certainty is unavailable.
explanations.B: Shell game: the premise about certainty is left untouched; it is the recommendation drawn from it that is attacked.
explanations.C: The philosopher traces the advice to its consistent application, finds the results unlivable, and rejects the advice on that basis. This is rejection by unacceptable consequences.
explanations.D: Half right: the argument does concern living by the advice, but the claim is that 'no one can' do so, an impossibility, not that its proponents hypocritically fail to.
explanations.E: Out of scope: no positive account of justification is offered.

keyTakeaway: 'If we followed this consistently... no one can live that way' is a reductio of a recommendation: the premises are granted and the consequences do the work.
predictionHint: Rejects the advice because its consistent application is unlivable.

stimulus: Statistician: My colleague objects that my model cannot be trusted because it was calibrated on data from only one decade. But her own preferred model was calibrated on data from a single, atypical year, and she regards that model as reliable. If a narrow calibration period disqualifies my model, it disqualifies hers all the more; and if it does not disqualify hers, it cannot disqualify mine. Either way, her objection fails.
stem: The statistician's argument proceeds by

choices.A: showing that the objection rests on a misunderstanding of how the statistician's model was calibrated
choices.B: demonstrating that the statistician's model is reliable despite its narrow calibration period
choices.C: accusing the colleague of applying to others a standard that she does not apply to herself
choices.D: arguing that the standard invoked by the objection either undermines the objector's own position or fails to undermine the position objected to
choices.E: establishing that models calibrated on a single atypical year are less reliable than models calibrated on a decade

explanations.A: Out of scope: the statistician accepts the colleague's description of the calibration period.
explanations.B: Shell game: the conclusion is that 'her objection fails,' not that the model is reliable; nothing positive about the model's reliability is established.
explanations.C: Half right: the colleague's inconsistency is noted, but the argument does not rest on the accusation. The 'If... and if...' structure shows the objection fails whichever way the standard is applied, regardless of what the colleague herself does.
explanations.D: The argument is a dilemma over the calibration standard: either it applies, in which case the colleague's model falls first, or it does not, in which case the statistician's model survives. Both horns defeat the objection.
explanations.E: Wrong part: the comparison 'all the more' is used inside one horn of the dilemma as a premise, not established as the conclusion.

keyTakeaway: 'If X, then...; and if not X, then...; either way' is a dilemma; describe the two horns, not just the hypocrisy that one horn exposes.
predictionHint: Dilemma: the standard either sinks her model too or sinks neither.
